transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what finally got me here was… I lost my temper. I was helping out with the volunteers, and one of the younger ones had put a tablecloth on crooked—just a tablecloth, mind you—and I just blew up at him. Snapped at him in front of everyone.

I don’t usually talk to people that way. I mean, I’ve run church suppers and school fundraisers and all sorts of things over the years, and crooked tablecloths happen. My wife used to say I could smooth anything over with a joke. But this time I didn’t. I went sharp, mean even, and afterward I thought, “That’s not like me.” So… that’s why I came in.
When you say 'that's not like me', how long have you been feeling like you're not yourself?

About a week, I’d say. Since that robbery outside the bank.

Funny thing is, I’ve gone to that bank for years—same branch, same little parking lot, they used to have a teller there who knew my wife by name. But yes… since that happened, I haven’t felt quite like myself. A week or so.
Have you been feeling anxious since the robbery happened?

Anxious… I don’t know if I’d use that word exactly. I mean, I’ve been unsettled, sure, but anxious sounds like… well, my sister used to get herself worked up before traveling, had to check her suitcase three times and all that.

For me it’s more that things feel a little off since then. I haven’t really sat down and named it. I suppose that’s part of why I’m here, to sort out what’s what.
Have you noticed any changes in your overall personality or the way you interact with others since the robbery?

Yes… I think so. Not my whole personality, maybe, but I’ve been sharper with people. What brought me in was that I blew up at one of the younger volunteers over a crooked tablecloth, and that’s just—well, I don’t usually talk to people that way.

I’ve worked with volunteers for years, you know, and there’s always some little thing out of place. Usually I’d just fix it or make some silly comment and move on. But this time I got mean about it, and afterward I felt embarrassed. So yes, I suppose the way I’m interacting with people has changed some.
Would you describe yourself as generally perfectionistic or critical of others before this incident with the volunteer?

I’m not sure I’d say perfectionistic, no. I mean, I like things done decently—if you’re setting up a room, you want the chairs straight enough so folks don’t trip, that sort of thing. My father was the real stickler in the family; he’d notice if a picture frame was off by a hair.

As for being critical… I don’t think people would’ve called me that, but you’d have to ask them, I suppose. I’ve had opinions like anybody. I just don’t know that I was especially hard on people before.
Have you been feeling sad or depressed since the robbery happened?

Sad or depressed… I don’t know. I mean, I wouldn’t say I’ve been sitting around weeping or anything like that. It’s funny, my mother used to say “low spirits” when someone was down, and I never quite knew what counted as that versus just having a bad week.

Since the robbery, I’ve had moments where I feel… off, I suppose. But sad? Depressed? I’m not sure I’d put that name on it.
Have you been having any recurring thoughts or urges to repeat certain behaviors since the robbery happened?

Recurring thoughts or urges to repeat behaviors… I’m not sure I follow exactly. Like checking the locks over and over, or doing something a certain number of times?

I haven’t noticed anything like that, not that I can think of. I mean, after something like that happens you do think about how things are set up, and whether you should’ve done this or that—but my wife always used to say I could overthink how to make a sandwich if left alone long enough. So I don’t know if that counts.

But no, I can’t say I’ve had some urge to repeat a behavior, no.
Have you been having any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind since the robbery happened?

Yes… yes, I suppose that does happen. It’s not like I’m sitting there trying to think about it, but out of nowhere I’ll hear that man’s rough voice in my head again. Or I’ll see that donation envelope hitting the floor.

It can happen when I’m just sitting at the kitchen table, not doing anything in particular. I’ll be looking at the salt shaker or the mail or whatever, and there it is. Strange how the mind does that. My wife used to keep the table so tidy—well, tidier than I do now—but anyway, yes, those bits of it do keep coming back.
Have you been feeling irritable most of the time since the robbery happened?

Irritable most of the time? I don’t know if I’d say most of the time. But… yes, I suppose I’ve been shorter with people.

Actually, that’s part of what got me to come in here. I snapped at one of the younger volunteers over a tablecloth being crooked. A tablecloth, of all things. I don’t usually talk to people that way. My wife was always the one who noticed when I was getting sharp—she’d give me that look across the room, you know—but I caught myself after, and I felt pretty ashamed.
Have you been avoiding places or situations that remind you of the robbery?

Yes… I have, I suppose. I’ve been taking the long way around town so I don’t have to pass the bank. It adds a few minutes, which is silly at my age—well, I’ve got time, don’t I—but I still do it.

And I haven’t gone into the festival storage room since then. I keep meaning to, because there are things in there that probably need sorting, old banners and folding chairs and Lord knows what else. My wife used to say every church storage room has at least three broken coffee urns hiding in it. But when I think about going in there, it just brings the whole thing too close again, so I don’t.
Are there any other places or activities you've been avoiding since the robbery happened?

Mostly it’s those same two, really—the bank and that festival storage room.

I’ve been going the long way around so I don’t have to pass the bank. It’s a bit ridiculous, I know, taking extra streets like that, but once you get used to a route… well, I tell myself I’m just getting some different scenery. And the storage room, I still haven’t gone back in there. I ought to, there are probably boxes piled up every which way, and someone will be looking for those old donation signs sooner or later. But when I picture opening that door, it just feels too close again, so I leave it be.
Have you been avoiding social gatherings or events since the robbery happened?

Yes… I suppose I have. I stopped going to card nights, and I used to enjoy those. Well, mostly enjoy them—there’s always one fellow who thinks he’s playing in Las Vegas instead of a church basement. But lately I just don’t feel steady around people, if that makes sense.

And the Día de los Muertos event… I’m still supposed to be helping organize it, like I usually do, but I haven’t been keeping up with it. There are lists and calls and decorations to sort out, and normally I’d be on top of that. This year I keep letting things sit. So yes, I guess I’ve been pulling back from gatherings some.
Have you been feeling guilty about anything related to the robbery?

Guilty? I… I’m not sure I’d call it that. I’ve thought it over, of course. You replay things in your head, same as when you leave the house and wonder if you turned off the stove—my wife used to check the stove twice, every time, drove me a little mad but she was usually right.

But guilt… no, I don’t know. I don’t think I have a clear answer there. I mostly just wish it hadn’t happened.
Have you noticed any problems with your work or daily activities since the robbery happened?

Yes, I suppose so. I’m not working anymore, so it’s not work in that sense, but the things I usually keep up with… I haven’t been doing them right.

The Día de los Muertos event, for instance—I’m usually the one making calls and keeping track of what needs doing, and this year I keep letting it slip. I’ll look at the list and then somehow I’m making tea or straightening a drawer instead. And I’ve stopped going to card nights too, which used to be part of my routine. I just don’t feel quite steady around people right now.
Are there any other activities or places that you've been avoiding since the robbery, besides the bank and the festival storage room?

Well, yes… mostly those two, I suppose. The bank, certainly—I’ve been taking the long way round so I don’t have to pass it. Adds a few minutes, which is silly at my age, because you’d think I’d be glad for the extra walk, though my knee doesn’t always agree.

And the festival storage room… no, I haven’t gone back in there. I know there are boxes in there that probably need sorting, candles and paper flowers and all that, but it just brings the whole thing too close. I keep finding some other errand to do instead.
Have you noticed any significant difficulties in your relationships with family or friends since the robbery happened?

Yes… a little, I suppose. I haven’t been as available to people. I used to help keep the Día de los Muertos event moving along—calls, lists, all the little things people forget until the last minute. My wife always said I liked a clipboard too much, which maybe I did.

But lately I don’t keep up with it the way I usually do. And I’ve stopped going to card nights. Those fellows have known me for years, so it isn’t that they’ve done anything wrong. I just don’t feel quite steady around people right now, and then I stay home, and then it’s harder to explain the next week.
Have you been easily startled since the robbery happened?

Yes… more than I’d like to admit. The other day outside the senior center, a car backfired—just a loud bang, nothing really—and I jumped so hard my chest actually hurt. My hands were shaking for a few minutes after.

Funny thing is, I used to complain about those old cars when I was younger, all the noise they made, and now here I am being scared half to death by one. I tried to laugh it off, but… yes, I’d say I’m more jumpy.
Have you been trying to avoid thinking about the robbery or memories related to it?

Yes… I think I have been. I mean, I don’t sit there and say, “Now I’m going to avoid thinking about it,” but I do things so it doesn’t come up.

Like I’ve been taking the long way around so I don’t have to pass the bank. It’s not even that far out of the way, really—past Mrs. Alvarez’s old house, if you know where that is, though she moved years ago. And I haven’t gone into the festival storage room either. There’s nothing dangerous in there, just boxes and decorations, but it brings the whole thing too close, and I’d rather not have those memories stirred up.
Have you felt like the changes in your behavior or mood since the robbery have significantly impacted your ability to function in your daily life or relationships?

Yes… I’d say it has, though I don’t like making it sound bigger than it is. I’m still getting through the day, you know, making coffee, keeping the house in order enough. But the things I’m usually counted on for, I haven’t been doing right.

The Día de los Muertos event, for example—I used to keep track of calls and lists and who was bringing what. I had a whole system, little notes everywhere, drove my wife crazy. This year I just… I can’t keep up with it the same way. And I’ve stopped going to card nights too. Those men are friends, good men, but I don’t feel steady around people right now, so I stay home. Then after a while it starts feeling awkward to go back.

doctor.question: Have you felt like the changes in your behavior or mood since the robbery have significantly impacted your ability to function in your daily life or relationships?

target_item.manifestation: I haven't been able to keep up with organizing the Día de los Muertos event the way I usually do, and I've stopped going to card nights because I don't feel steady around people right now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether symptoms have significantly impacted daily functioning or relationships, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes… I’d say it has, though I don’t like making it sound bigger than it is. I’m still getting through the day, you know, making coffee, keeping the house in order enough. But the things I’m usually counted on for, I haven’t been doing right.

The Día de los Muertos event, for example—I used to keep track of calls and lists and who was bringing what. I had a whole system, little notes everywhere, drove my wife crazy. This year I just… I can’t keep up with it the same way. And I’ve stopped going to card nights too. Those men are friends, good men, but I don’t feel steady around people right now, so I stay home. Then after a while it starts feeling awkward to go back.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms, including avoidance of reminders of the robbery, irritability, and difficulty sleeping (implied by being 'jumpy' and having an exaggerated startle response), along with significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, suggest a diagnosis of Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
